title: Transfluxor-style ferroelectric column gate eliminates repair comparators
idea: The 1956 transfluxor used flux stored around a control aperture to block or pass transfer through a second aperture. Put one HZO ferroelectric FET in series with each column-select line. Programmed at wafer test, a bad column's FeFET stays permanently off and its spare's turns on, so column repair needs no fuse-address comparators in the read path.
why: Removes column-redundancy compare logic and fuse latches (fact 7) and shaves ~0.5-1 ns off the column access path.

title: Vibrating-reed electrometer screens leakage-tail cells in milliseconds
idea: The 1940s vibrating-reed electrometer measured femtoamps by modulating a capacitor mechanically. A varactor-modulated test capacitor on each mat's test bus measures each row's integrated leakage directly by lock-in detection in milliseconds, replacing hours-long hot retention tests. Rows are then binned into 2-4 refresh classes stored on the die.
why: Enables per-row refresh where today the ≤13 fA tail forces worst-case refresh for every row (fact 3), cutting refresh ~60-75%, and slashes test time.

title: Po: wordlines on springs — stepwise adiabatic charge-recycling drivers
idea: Po: a wordline that bounces back for free. Drive each global/main wordline through a stepwise adiabatic charger, 4-6 on-die tank capacitors switched in sequence, so the ~3 V wordline rises and falls in small steps and returns most of its charge to the tanks instead of dumping it to ground.
why: Voltage floor (#10): wordline CV^2 energy falls ~60-75%, which also unloads the VPP charge pump and shrinks it (periphery #7).

title: Alien trits: three-level cells read in pairs as three bits
idea: An alien that never learned binary stores three charge levels per cell. Two cells are read together by a two-threshold sense amp (two staggered latches with +/-1/3 references), and their 9 joint states encode 3 bits.
why: 1.5 bits per capacitor (+50% density, lower cost per bit) without a new cell, paid for with ~3x tighter sense margin that needs offset-cancelled SAs (fact 1).

title: Wide-and-slow periphery lets U.S. 65 nm logic drive DRAM
idea: Reverse speed for width: the array die exposes 8x more data bonds at 1/8 the clock (e.g., 4096 bits at 800 MT/s) to a face-bonded base die from a U.S. 65-90 nm fab; serialization happens only on the host link.
why: Facts 5 and 7: high-speed periphery that forces advanced nodes disappears from the DRAM; I/O energy ~0.5 pJ/bit.

title: Resonant bitline reads the stored bit as a frequency shift
idea: Reverse voltage sensing into frequency sensing: each bitline forms part of a resonator; turning on the access transistor loads it with the cell's state-dependent MOS-varactor capacitance, and one wideband counter reads the detuning of 64 bitlines tuned to separate tones.
why: Facts 7 and 8: one reader replaces 64 SAs, and a probe amplitude far below the stored voltage makes the read non-destructive, eliminating restore energy.

title: Merging: dual-gate access devices decode 1024 rows with 64 drivers
idea: TRIZ #5 Merging moves the last decode stage into the cells: each oxide-TFT access device has a bottom gate tied to a group plate (32 groups) and a top gate tied to an in-group line strapped across groups (32 lines), and conducts only when both are high, so 1024 wordlines need 64 drivers instead of 1024 sub-wordline drivers.
why: 100x path: wordline-driver area falls ~16x and the remaining periphery fits under one tier, making 8-16 stacked TFT tiers on a mature logic base viable; trade-offs: half-selected cells need a strong dual-gate threshold shift and see more disturb, and wordline RC is slower. Attacks Fact 7.

title: Fleet-learned per-bank sense timing and voltage from hyperscaler telemetry
idea: Hyperscalers are extreme users with millions of DIMMs: expose per-bank trim registers for tRCD, sense delay, VARY and refresh rate, and let a fleet model trained on correctable-error events and temperature push tuned settings to each die over its life.
why: Recovers ~15-25% latency and energy margin designed for worst-case silicon, and raises usable supply by keeping marginal dies in service.

title: Sputtered IGZO thin-film decoders stacked above the cell array
idea: Substitute crystalline-silicon row decoders with sputtered IGZO TFT decoders built at <=350 C on top of the array (ALD HfO2 gate, Mo source/drain). A university nanofab can demonstrate a 64-row decoder over a MIM-cap test array with i-line lithography.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): moving decode above the array reclaims ~10-15% of die; low-temperature BEOL process, no EUV.

title: Image-sensor correlated double sampling for bitline sensing
idea: Borrowed from CMOS image sensors: a switched-capacitor column comparator samples the bitline onto one small cap right after precharge (capturing kTC reset noise, random-telegraph noise and its own offset) and onto a second cap after the wordline opens, then decides on the difference. Everything common to both samples subtracts out.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): cuts required signal margin ~40-50%, so Cs can fall from ~5 fF to ~3 fF or bitlines can double in length (half the sense amps).

title: Stacked image-sensor Cu-Cu bonding gives every bitline segment a sense amp
idea: Borrowed from Sony's pixel-parallel stacked image sensors: the array wafer is bonded face-to-face to a logic wafer at ~1 um pitch so each 32-64-cell bitline segment connects to its own sense amp below, eliminating long bitlines.
why: Charge wall: bitline capacitance drops ~10x, so ~0.5 fF or capacitorless cells work, and sense-amp stripes leave the array die (~15% area).

title: CCD bucket-brigade shifts row charge to one edge sense node
idea: Like a CCD image sensor, each mat's bitlines become buried-channel charge-transfer registers: an activated row dumps its packets into the channel, and clock phases march them to one high-gain floating-diffusion amplifier at the mat edge, read serially and restored through a write-back register. One sense chain serves 16 columns.
why: Periphery area: SA count falls 16x (SA stripes ~20% of die to ~3%); serial readout matches HBM bursts, and only burst bits are moved, which cuts overfetch.

title: Image-sensor single-slope ramp ADC reads two bits per cell
idea: Copy the CMOS image sensor's column ADC: one global ramp generator per bank plus a 6-transistor comparator and 2-bit counter latch per bitline turn the developed bitline voltage into one of 4 levels; restore writes back one of 4 voltages from shared DAC rails.
why: Cost per bit: 2 bits/cell is ~1.8x bits per wafer for ~12% more SA area; the ramp is shared, so periphery per bit falls.

title: Column-parallel single-slope ramp sensing reads two bits per cell
idea: Borrow image-sensor column ADCs: one global ramp shared by 8k columns, a tiny comparator plus 3-bit counter per column digitizes the bitline twice (precharge and signal) and subtracts digitally (digital CDS). Offset and kT/C cancel in the subtraction, giving enough resolution to store 4 charge levels per cell.
why: Density/cost per bit: 2 bits/cell = ~2x bits per array area without litho shrink (fact 4); offset no longer sets the minimum signal.

title: Vertical CCD charge-shift columns with one floating-diffusion sense node
idea: Box: potential-well storage in poly-Si/IGZO channel x CCD transfer gates x floating-diffusion source follower x 3D vertical stack x Si x CMOS image-sensor fab. Bits are charge packets that shift up one tier per clock to a single sense node at the top, like an image sensor's vertical register, so tiers need no individual wordline decoders or staircase contacts.
why: 3D DRAM blocker plus periphery: per-tier decoders and staircases vanish; uses U.S. CIS fabs; suits page-oriented ~100 ns access.

title: Po: read cells like a camera — single-slope ternary ADC
idea: Po: memory read like an image sensor. Store three charge levels per cell; a bank-wide voltage ramp and a counter are broadcast to all columns, and each column comparator latches the count when its bitline crosses the ramp, exactly as CMOS image-sensor column ADCs do, then a 2-bit column DAC restores the level.
why: Density and capacitor wall (#1): 1.58 bits per capacitor pillar (~50% more bits per array area); the shared ramp/counter keeps per-column overhead to one comparator and a small latch.

title: Floating-diffusion charge-transfer readout for sub-femtofarad slow tier
idea: Scale-shift the image-sensor floating diffusion into DRAM and slow it down: a gated transfer transistor moves the bitline's charge onto a ~0.05 fF sense node over ~200-500 ns, giving voltage gain of ~Cbl/Cfd, which makes 0.3-0.5 fF planar cells readable as a ~1 us capacity tier.
why: No high-AR capacitor (fact 1) and fewer HAR/EUV steps (fact 4); ~2-3x bits per mask set for a capacity tier behind HBM.

title: Si: CCD bucket-brigade bitlines feeding one floating-diffusion amplifier
idea: Borrow the image-sensor trick: after a row opens, each cell's charge is clocked as a packet along a buried-channel silicon bitline to one ~1 fF floating-diffusion source follower plus comparator shared by 32-64 columns; restore is a reverse shift of a regenerated packet.
why: A ~1 fF sense node versus a ~60 fF bitline gives 10-50x more volts per electron, relaxing the Cs wall (fact 1) and cutting sense-amp count ~30x (fact 7); the cost is shift latency, suited to streaming or HBM-like page reads.

title: No column decoder: CCD-style shift-out of the latched row
idea: Limit: no column decoder and no global column-select lines. After sensing, the sense amps are linked by two pass transistors each into a dynamic shift register that clocks the row out serially toward taps placed every 256 bits at the bank edge, like a CCD image sensor; random column access becomes 'shift N from the nearest tap'.
why: Periphery (fact 7): column decoders plus CSL wiring take ~5-8% of the die and one metal layer; streaming readout suits AI tensor fetches.

title: Goto-pair Esaki tunnel-diode latch as sense amplifier
idea: Substitute the cross-coupled inverter latch with a Goto pair: two series Esaki tunnel diodes whose negative differential resistance forms a bistable node that the bitline signal tips one way. Degenerately doped Si or uni-MBE InGaAs junctions are within university reach.
why: Speed and energy: NDR latching switches in ps at ~0.3 V, cutting sense energy and allowing lower array voltage (fact 10).

title: Esaki tunnel-diode Goto-pair latches at bitline pitch
idea: The 1959 Goto pair used two series tunnel diodes as a bistable logic element. One added pocket-implant mask forms p++/n++ Esaki junctions at each sense node, and two in series make a negative-resistance latch that resolves a bitline differential in tens of picoseconds with 2 devices instead of a 4-6 transistor cross-coupled pair.
why: The sense amp fits at 1x bitline pitch in open-bitline arrays, roughly halving the sense stripe (fact 7) and cutting latch energy.

title: Esaki tunnel-diode Goto pair as a static one-transistor cell
idea: Inverting 'a DRAM cell stores charge': two series interband tunnel diodes form a bistable node via negative differential resistance, gated onto the bitline by one access transistor, and the node already sits at one of two latched levels so the column needs only a simple comparator.
why: Static storage with no refresh and no capacitor at ~1T area, with nA hold current; diode peak-current uniformity at scale is the risk.

title: Crystal radio: tunnel-diode Goto-pair sense amp biased at 0.2 V
idea: A crystal radio works with almost no power. Build each sense amp as a Goto pair, two series Esaki tunnel diodes (e.g., Si/SiGe or III-V on the periphery wafer) biased in their negative-resistance region at ~0.2 V; the bitline signal tips the pair into one of two stable states within picoseconds, with no high-voltage cross-coupled latch.
why: SA latch energy scales with V2: 0.2 V instead of ~1 V is ~25x less latch energy and allows a low-swing bitline; 10x on sensing energy even after diode peak-current overhead; risk is diode uniformity and integration.

title: Interference lithography for arrays, multibeam e-beam for periphery
idea: Reverse which region gets premium patterning: perfectly periodic array lines are printed by simple laser interference lithography (buildable in the U.S.) and pitch-split with U.S.-made deposition/etch, while the sparse, irregular periphery layers are written maskless by U.S.-built multi-column e-beam.
why: Fact 4: replaces 5-7 EUV layers and mask sets with an all-U.S. toolchain, removing the single-supplier EUV dependency.

title: Measure first, wire last: e-beam personalizes each wafer's periphery
idea: Reverse design-then-build: after array test, a U.S.-built multibeam e-beam writes the final periphery metal per wafer, setting SA reference trims, bitline segmentation and timing taps to that wafer's measured leakage and Cs distribution.
why: Facts 3 and 7: per-wafer tuned margins cut refresh ~30-50% and add ~5-10% yield, deleting on-die trim and fuse circuits.

title: Firefly anti-phase coupled oscillators that self-spread refresh bursts
idea: Pulse-coupled fireflies with inhibitory coupling settle into anti-phase. Each bank's local refresh oscillator senses neighbors' refresh current on a shared line and delays itself when they fire, so refresh bursts spread evenly in time across banks with no central scheduler.
why: Peak refresh current sets power-grid metal, decap area and IR-drop margin. Spreading cuts peak current 4-8x, letting grid and decaps shrink (~2-3% of die).

title: Frozen periphery platform wafer reused for three array generations
idea: Hybrid-bond each new array wafer onto a standardized 28 nm periphery wafer whose bond interface and protocol are frozen for 6+ years, so a new node needs only array masks: MAGNIFY the periphery's lifetime, MINIFY per-node mask and EUV spend.
why: Facts 4 and 7: per-node capex -30-40%; periphery wafers can come from existing U.S. trailing-edge fabs, raising U.S. content.

title: Particle-detector zero suppression for sparse data bursts
idea: Borrowed from LHC detector readout zero suppression: each column group computes a wired-OR nonzero flag during sensing, and bytes that are all zero are sent as a 1-bit tag instead of toggling global data lines and I/O drivers.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): AI activations and KV caches are 30-60% zero bytes, so global-bus and I/O energy drop ~25-45% for <1% area.

title: Panel laser-and-inkjet repair replaces fuse-based redundancy
idea: Borrowed from OLED and LCD line-repair stations: bitlines or wordlines found defective by in-line test are laser-cut and bridged to spare lines with inkjet-printed silver jumpers, so the glass memory needs no fuse banks or redundancy address comparators.
why: Periphery and yield: removes ~3% of area for redundancy logic and rescues large panel regions that a single defect would otherwise scrap.

title: Xerographic bitlines: light-switched photoconductive segments shorten bitlines on demand
idea: Borrow the photocopier drum: build each bitline from segments joined by amorphous-silicon photoconductor bridges that insulate in the dark. An on-chip SiN waveguide fed by an off-chip laser lights only the bridges between the accessed segment and the SA, so the SA sees a short, low-capacitance line and the rest is electrically absent.
why: Bitline capacitance per access falls 4-8x, multiplying the signal: Cs could drop from ~5 fF to ~1-2 fF (breaking the charge wall), with one SA serving very long bitlines.

title: Vacuum nanogap transistors as oxide-free high-voltage drivers
idea: Revive the vacuum tube at 50 nm. One added cavity mask etches a nanogap between a sharp source tip and the drain under an existing gate, and a non-conformal oxide deposition pinches it shut under vacuum. Field emission across a gap shorter than the electron mean free path switches with no gate-oxide stress and tolerates 3-5 V at minimum size.
why: Wordline and pump switches no longer need large thick-oxide HV transistors (facts 7, 10), so driver area could shrink ~3x; a radiation-hard bonus for space.

title: MIM-feedback charge amplifier sense with geometry-set gain
idea: Hold the bitline at virtual ground with a compact cascode integrator whose gain is Q/Cf, set by a MIM capacitor ratio rather than transistor Vt or mobility, so the output is independent of Cbl, temperature and aging.
why: Cbl no longer divides signal (fact 1): ~3-5x more output per electron, stable over 10 y at 125 C; longer bitlines cut SA count.

title: Particle-detector charge amplifier holds bitline at virtual ground
idea: Like LHC pixel ASICs that read ~1000-electron hits in 25 ns, each sense stripe uses a folded-cascode charge-sensitive amplifier that clamps the bitline at virtual ground and integrates the full cell charge onto a ~1 fF feedback capacitor, so the output is Qcell/Cf instead of Qcell/(Cs+Cbl). Bitline capacitance drops out of the signal equation.
why: Charge wall and periphery area: a signal independent of Cbl lets bitlines be 2-4x longer (2-4x fewer SAs, ~10-15% die saved) or Cs ~3x smaller.

title: Two-terminal ovonic threshold switches replace bitline equalize transistors
idea: Substitute the three-transistor precharge/equalize block with sputtered GeSe-class ovonic threshold switches between bitline pairs and the precharge rail, fired by a short overdrive pulse.
why: Periphery area: equalizers sit at bitline pitch in vias rather than in active silicon, freeing ~10% of the sense strip.

title: Po: bitlines never precharge — rail-held transition sensing
idea: Po: bitlines that never return to VDD/2. Each bitline stays at the full rail left by the last restore; on the next activation an AC-coupled detector sees either no step (new bit equals held rail) or a full charge-sharing step, and the latch, knowing the held rail, decodes 'same/different' into the new bit.
why: Destructive read (#8) energy: removes equalization and tRP (~14 ns), and bitlines only swing when consecutive rows differ, ~50% bitline energy saving on random data and more on correlated data.

title: Resonant LC energy recovery for bitline precharge and restore
idea: Substitute dissipative CMOS precharge and restore with adiabatic swing: banks of bitlines are switched onto an in-package inductor so their charge rings sinusoidally between two bank groups instead of being dumped to ground and recharged from VDD.
why: Energy per bit (fact 10): bitline CV^2 dominates activate energy, and resonant recovery of 50-70% of that charge cuts activate/restore energy about 2x without lowering VARY.

title: Ion-exchanged glass waveguides form the panel's global data bus
idea: Borrowed from ion-exchange waveguides used in planar fiber couplers: optical waveguides are written into the glass substrate itself, with microLED emitters at each mat and thin-film photodiodes at the panel edge replacing centimeter-long metal global I/O lines.
why: Data movement on large panels: long-wire CV2 energy becomes ~0.1-0.5 pJ/bit optical links, with no extra wiring layers since the waveguide is inside the substrate.

title: Andon-cord sense amps flag slow-resolving cells for targeted refresh
idea: Like Toyota's andon cord, which any worker pulls to flag a problem, each SA strip gets a tiny resolution-time detector (XOR of the latch nodes sampled at a fixed delay after enable). Any SA still metastable at the strobe pulls a shared andon line, so the controller logs that row as weak and refreshes it more often while others refresh less.
why: Finds weak, leaky cells during normal traffic with no test overhead; most rows can run 4-8x longer refresh intervals, cutting refresh energy (~46 fJ/bit) and bandwidth loss ~60-75%.

title: Po: array runs on 0.4 V — Marx-stacked bitline sampling
idea: Po: an array that runs on 0.4 V. Drop VARY to ~0.4 V; after charge sharing, the bitline differential is sampled onto four small capacitors in parallel, which are then switched into series like a Marx generator, presenting ~4x the voltage to a latch that restores to 0.4 V.
why: Voltage floor (#10): array CV^2 energy falls ~6x vs 1 V while the Marx stack recovers the voltage margin lost to the low swing.

title: Canary columns detect row hammer and hot retention together
idea: Reserve ~8 columns per row holding a known pattern written at a deliberately weaker level; whenever the row is opened (access or refresh) the SAs check the canaries for free. A flipped canary means the row's neighbors are hammered or leakage at 125 C is outrunning refresh, triggering targeted refresh.
why: Row hammer (fact 9) and retention (fact 3) monitored with ~0.1% area and no counters; physics-tracking at any temperature.

title: Radiant floor tiles: sense amps under array enable short, low-voltage bitlines
idea: Lay sense amps under the mats like heating tiles under a floor, on a logic layer joined by 0.3-0.5 um-pitch hybrid bonds (one per bitline), so bitlines shrink from ~512 to ~128 cells; the ~4x lower C_BL triples read signal, and that margin is spent cutting VARY from 1.0 V to ~0.5 V.
why: Bitline energy scales with C_BL x VARY2: 4x lower C times 4x lower V2 gives ~10-16x less array energy per activation, and SA area stops costing die area (fact 7).

title: Eliminate sub-wordline drivers: resonant LC wordlines with energy recovery
idea: Delete the sub-wordline driver stripes by making master wordlines low-resistance Ru lines that a single pass switch per row connects to a bank-wide resonant LC rail. The switch closes at the sinusoid trough and opens at its peak, so the wordline charges adiabatically and most of its energy returns to the tank on discharge.
why: SWD stripes are ~8-10% of the die. Adiabatic charging recovers ~60-70% of wordline CV2 energy, which is stuck by the 3 V wordline (fact 10).

title: Ship lightly repaired dies with exported bad-row maps, NAND-style
idea: Worse: scrap any die whose defects exceed on-die fuse and spare-row capacity, and keep growing redundancy area. Flip: ship dies with minimal spares plus an exported defect and weak-row map that the memory controller uses to remap rows, the way NAND controllers handle bad blocks.
why: Periphery area (fact 7) and supply: shrinks fuse/spare area 2-3% and recovers 5-15% of discarded dies, directly raising usable bit supply.

title: Printed nanoparticle varistor film takes over ESD protection duty
idea: Worse: guard every I/O pad with large on-die ESD clamps that add capacitance and area. Flip: screen-print a ZnO-nanoparticle varistor film between I/O traces and ground on the package substrate so surges clamp off-die, letting on-die clamps shrink to minimal size.
why: Periphery area and I/O energy: smaller clamps cut pad capacitance ~30-50% and free I/O ring area.

title: Printed micro-heater film for fast wafer-level retention binning
idea: Worse: profile retention with slow chamber bakes so rows are never binned individually. Flip: laminate a printed resistive heater film at the probe-chuck interface that steps each die through precise temperatures in seconds while BIST logs per-row retention, storing bins for retention-aware refresh.
why: Refresh (fact 3): cheap per-row retention bins enable 2-4x longer refresh for most rows.

title: 77 K drawer in each rack holds long-lived data refresh-free
idea: Scale jump to rack infrastructure: one liquid-nitrogen-cooled drawer per rack hosts DRAM whose leakage at 77 K gives hours-to-days retention, with sense amps re-centered for cryogenic Vt and lower offset; warm DRAM keeps hot data while the cold drawer holds embedding tables and long-lived state with refresh disabled.
why: Zero refresh power (fact 3) and faster cryo periphery; the ~10 W-per-W cooling overhead restricts it to capacity-heavy, low-access data.

title: Dropped-stitch knitting: token-chained subarrays replace fuse-compare redundancy
idea: Like a knitter passing over a dropped stitch, a token threads through every subarray at power-up (the Catt-spiral idea from 1989 Anamartic wafer-scale memory). A subarray that fails its built-in self-test simply passes the token on, so the chain itself builds the address map with no fuse banks or address comparators.
why: Removes most fuse arrays and redundancy comparators (~3-6% of die) and gives coarse subarray sparing that tolerates clustered defects, raising yield at 180 nm and above.

title: Kerf-resident test periphery lives in scribe lanes
idea: Test-only circuits (BIST engines, test compression, probe pads) are used once but occupy die forever. Place them in the 60-100 um scribe lanes, wired to each die through traces that are severed at dicing, leaving only a minimal test port on the die.
why: Recovers ~2-4% of die area per wafer at zero process change (fact 7), more bits per wafer = lower cost per bit.

title: Move DFT and BIST logic onto an active probe-card ASIC
idea: Box: any cell x any access x any SA x test logic off-die x bulk Si x probe-card ASIC. Built-in self-test engines, test-mode decoders and compression logic leave each DRAM die and live on a reusable active probe card that drives a minimal raw test port.
why: Periphery -2-4% per die forever, paid once per probe card; faster test too.

title: Qi-style inductive coupling stacks glass memory sheets without vias
idea: Borrowed from wireless charging and NFC coils: thin glass memory sheets are laminated with planar coils at each I/O site, passing data and clock inductively through glass, which unlike silicon has no eddy-current loss.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): no TSV or through-glass-via keep-out area or yield loss, and stacking is just lamination at ~1-2 pJ/bit per vertical link.

title: Atom-switch rewiring makes decoder redundancy field-reprogrammable
idea: Ideal result: wiring that can be redrawn after shipment. Place Cu-ion bridge (atom) switches in the BEOL between decoder outputs and spare wordline drivers; a field repair command forms or dissolves bridges to remap any row to any spare, repeatedly.
why: Repair: replaces one-shot laser or e-fuses with reversible rewiring, extending module life and salvaging aging parts.

title: Cochlea-style dithered repeated comparisons beat sense-amp offset
idea: The ear's hair cells detect sub-noise sounds with help from noise. A tiny clocked comparator, isolated from the bitline, fires 7 times before and 7 times after the wordline rises while a known triangular dither is coupled in; the difference of the two vote counts cancels the comparator offset and resolves a signal below it, then the main latch restores.
why: Sense margin is offset-limited at ~15-20 mV; ~3x effective resolution lets Cs fall from ~5 fF toward ~2 fF, sidestepping the 60-75:1 aspect-ratio capacitor wall (fact 1).

title: Po: sense with the transistor DRAM abandoned — lateral Si BJT
idea: Po: a bipolar memory reader. Place a lateral npn preamp pair (boron/phosphorus-doped silicon only, no high-k, no metal gate) at each SA input; BJT Vbe matching (~0.3 mV sigma vs ~5 mV for small MOSFETs) and higher gm resolve millivolt signals before a cheap MOS latch.
why: Capacitor wall (#1) and periphery (#7): ~10x lower offset lets Cs drop ~40% or bitlines double in length (half the SA strips), using only Si, B, P.

title: Delete redundancy rows, columns and fuse banks; ECC absorbs defects
idea: Box: standard cell x Si access x standard SA x no repair periphery x bulk Si x shorter test flow. Defects and weak cells up to a 1% budget stay in place under the code, so spare rows and columns, redundancy compare logic, laser/e-fuse banks and repair test steps all go.
why: Periphery -3-5% of die, lower test cost and time, higher yield because defects stop scrapping dies.

title: Hub-and-spoke periphery die time-shared by four array dies
idea: Borrowed from airline and parcel hub-and-spoke networks: four periphery-free array dies (cells and local latches only) stack on one logic-process hub die holding decoders, pumps, refresh, I/O and test, linked by hybrid bonds; the hub serves whichever array is active.
why: Periphery ~49% (fact 7): amortizing periphery over four arrays lifts array efficiency from ~51% to ~80%+ and moves periphery to EUV-free mature logic.

title: Vacuum nanogap field-emission triodes as BEOL wordline drivers
idea: Effect: Fowler-Nordheim field emission in vacuum. Etch sealed ~50 nm vacuum cavities in BEOL with sharp Mo or TiN emitters (no tungsten); grid-gated emission switches ~3 V wordlines with no channel leakage and no thick-oxide HV transistors, stacking the driver bank above the array.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): HV sub-wordline driver strips are ~10% of die; moving them into BEOL could shrink the die ~8%.

title: Ni: nickel-silicide Schottky transistors make implant-free periphery logic
idea: Build periphery decoders from dopant-segregated NiSi Schottky-barrier MOSFETs formed by thermal silicidation, skipping ion implanters whose sources use argon dilution and purge; the abrupt metal junction shortens channels and limits short-channel leakage.
why: Removes ~10 implant masks and steps from periphery (capital, fact 4) and packs logic denser (fact 7) without rare gases.

title: Stepwise tank-capacitor charging makes bitline restore nearly adiabatic
idea: MAGNIFY on-die charge storage: bitline restore and equalization proceed in 4 steps through BEOL high-k tank capacitors (<=300 C) instead of one full swing from the supply, so each step dissipates only ~1/4 of the CV2/2 that a direct swing wastes.
why: Facts 8 and 10: array activation energy -25-35% without lowering voltages.

title: Array stores its own sense-amp offset trims, refreshed as charge
idea: Reverse who serves whom: at power-up BIST measures each SA's offset and writes 4-bit trims to a reserved row per subarray; at every refresh that row is read into tiny charge-storage trim capacitors at each SA, which bias the latch to cancel offset.
why: Fact 7: minimum-size SAs with offset trimmed to <3 mV; SA area ~-40% and required signal ~-30%, allowing smaller Cs.

title: Charge-injection-device cells: two-gate X-Y charge storage with non-destructive reads
idea: Failure mined: GE's charge-injection device (CID) imager lost to CCDs, yet it had an X-Y addressed, transistor-free pixel of two coupled MOS gates, read non-destructively by moving charge between the gates and sensing the column. Fix: use CID pairs as memory cells, with the row gate and column gate overlapping one storage well. A write injects charge; a read shifts it under the column gate and back, so the charge never leaves the well and can be re-read for multi-level sensing.
why: 10x at the same cost: a transistor-free ~4F^2 cell (1.5x) x 3 bits per well from averaged non-destructive re-reads (3x) x no restore and much less periphery (~2x) = ~9-10x, using planar CMOS-image-sensor processing.

title: Po: the barrier grows itself — CuMn wiring, no Ta/Co/Ru
idea: Po: copper wiring that makes its own diffusion barrier. Use a Cu-0.5%Mn seed; on anneal Mn migrates to the dielectric interface and forms a ~2 nm MnSiOx barrier, replacing PVD Ta/TaN and Co/Ru liners in all periphery metal levels, with plain Al for top global levels.
why: Scarce resources: removes Ta, Co and Ru from periphery BEOL; the thinner barrier also adds ~15-20% copper cross-section in narrow lines, cutting RC.

title: Thyristor columns where an inverter replaces the sense amp
idea: Inverting 'the cell signal is millivolts': vertical npnp thyristor cells latch on with ~10-30 uA read current versus pA off, so bitlines swing to the rail within ns and each column is read by a skewed inverter with a keeper; reads are nondestructive, so the restore phase disappears.
why: Periphery ~30% smaller (no latch sense amp, no half-VDD precharge, no restore) and tRC ~5 ns, with no capacitor to scale.

title: Burn-in tempering: stress each sense amp until its offset vanishes
idea: Like tempering steel with controlled heat, use the 1990s wafer-level burn-in oven to apply asymmetric hot-carrier stress to the stronger transistor of each SA pair, chosen by a built-in offset measurement. The stress shifts its Vt until the pair matches, and the trapped charge makes the shift permanent.
why: SA offset sigma drops ~2-3x with zero added area, allowing ~2x more cells per bitline (SA strips -50% of their ~12% die share) using only legacy burn-in equipment.

title: Taking out: transistor-free array dies time-share one CMOS reader die
idea: TRIZ #2 Taking out: array dies hold only capacitor cells, oxide-TFT access devices and a TFT 1024:1 bitline multiplexer, built with ~10 masks on depreciated 65-90 nm lines; 16 such dies stack on one 28 nm CMOS reader die whose sense amps, decoders and I/O serve every die through vertical global bitlines, one die active at a time.
why: 100x path: no front-end CMOS on 15/16 of the silicon (~3x), mature tools (~4x), periphery amortized 16x (~2x) and cheap stacking (~4x); trade-offs: ~1/16 bandwidth per stack, ~us row cycle and thermal limits. Attacks Facts 4 and 7 and U.S. manufacturability.

title: Hermit-crab DIMM: depreciated-node dies behind a translating buffer
idea: A hermit crab moves into an old shell. A module buffer chip presents standard DDR5 to the host but drives two interleaved ranks of older-node DDR4-class dies from fully depreciated fab lines, translating commands and refresh and matching DDR5 bandwidth with a few ns of added latency.
why: Depreciation is ~55% of wafer cost (fact 4); dies from paid-off lines can be ~40% cheaper per bit and that capacity exists today, raising supply fast.

title: Eliminate copper and tungsten: oxygen-patterned multilayer graphene periphery lines
idea: Grow 10-20-layer graphene on a Co catalyst at BEOL temperature, intercalation-dope it with FeCl3, and pattern it with O2 plasma, since carbon needs no halogen etch. The lines need no Ta/TaN barrier and resist electromigration.
why: Removes W (China ~80%), Cu and Ta from local periphery wiring with the simplest fluorine-free etch; at sub-30 nm widths doped graphene avoids copper's size-effect resistivity rise.

title: Thermal expansion: latching bimorph nano-relays as zero-leakage wordline decoders
idea: TRIZ #37 Thermal expansion: wordline decoders are built from bistable electrothermal bimorph nano-relays patterned in BEOL metal and oxide layers above the array, with no transistors; a heat pulse flexes a relay into contact where it latches mechanically, routing ~3 V wordline drive with zero off-state leakage.
why: 100x path: decoders move out of front-end silicon into ~4 cheap metal masks at 90 nm-class pitch, enabling transistor-free periphery over stacked arrays; trade-offs: ~0.1-1 us switching and relay wear (~1e9-1e12 cycles) limits activations per row. Attacks Facts 7 and 10.

title: Guide-star dummy bitline cancels mat-wide noise in real time
idea: Astronomers measure atmospheric blur on a guide star and subtract it. Each mat keeps a dummy bitline pair whose cell holds a known value; its deviation at sense time measures the instantaneous common disturbance, which is fed forward to every SA reference node in that mat within the same strobe.
why: Recovers ~20-30% of sense margin lost to correlated noise, spendable as longer bitlines or lower VARY (facts 1, 7, 10).

title: Intermediary: threshold-switch selector capacitor crossbar with edge-only periphery
idea: TRIZ #24 Intermediary: an ovonic threshold switch in series with each capacitor (1S1C) lets the capacitor charge or discharge only when the full row-column voltage exceeds the switch threshold, while half-selected cells stay isolated; arrays become transistor-free crossbars stacked 8 decks high in BEOL, with decoders and sense amps only at array edges.
why: 100x path: zero transistors in the array, ~2 masks per deck and periphery amortized over 8 decks on a mature-node base; trade-offs: sub-threshold selector leakage limits retention to ~ms (frequent refresh), selector endurance ~1e10-1e12 and higher read energy. Attacks Facts 2 and 4.

title: Drywall prefab: array wafers plus dry-bonded periphery chiplets
idea: Construction cut on-site water by moving from wet plaster to factory drywall. Keep only pitch-matched SAs on the array wafer and move the non-pitch-matched periphery (pumps, global decode, control, DLL, I/O) to 40 nm logic chiplets, bonded fluxless with formic-acid-vapor reflow and plasma activation, both dry steps.
why: Water: the array wafer skips the high-metal-count logic module, and the chiplets use few wet steps on ~1/3 the area, so water for that periphery falls ~10x; it also takes periphery off EUV.

title: Charge-transfer presensing doubles cells per bitline
idea: Revive 1990s charge-transfer presensing: a Vt-compensated transfer transistor between a long bitline and a small sense node amplifies the signal by the capacitance ratio, so 1,024 cells per bitline work and the number of SA stripes halves.
why: Periphery (fact 7): SA stripes are ~20-25% of die; halving them saves ~10% die area on existing processes.

title: Accumulative ferroelectric FET counts activations per row nonvolatilely
idea: Exploit accumulative partial switching in HZO/AlScN: each ACT applies a sub-coercive pulse to a per-row FeFET (<=400 C), nudging its threshold one step; after N steps it trips a neighbor-refresh flag and is reset, MINIFYING a row-hammer counter to one transistor.
why: Fact 9: exact per-row counts at ~0.5% area with no SRAM tables; FeFET endurance (~1e10 cycles) versus reset rate is the main risk.

title: Read the cell's EMF: electrochemical bits sensed by voltage
idea: Constraint: non-volatile with zero read current. Store bits as ion concentration in a nanoscale electrochemical (ECRAM-like) cell whose open-circuit voltage differs by ~100 mV between states; the SA samples that voltage onto a precharged floating bitline through a high-impedance gate, so the read draws no state-changing current.
why: Read disturb and read energy fall to ~0 (voltage, not current); non-destructive. Risk: ns-speed bitline charging from a high-impedance source.

title: Conductive ferroelectric domain walls give nondestructive reads
idea: Inverting 'ferroelectric reads are destructive': in thin-film lithium niobate cells, switching creates a conducting domain wall between electrodes, so the state is read as a 1e3-1e5 current ratio without switching the polarization.
why: Nondestructive, high-margin reads remove restore circuitry and refresh; uses a non-tungsten, non-EUV material stack; endurance of wall motion (~1e10+) must be proven.

title: Origami chip-on-flex stack folds dies around a printed shared bus
idea: Worse: stack dies rigidly with TSVs and microbumps. Flip: mount thin dies at intervals along a roll-to-roll-printed flex tape carrying a shared command and data bus plus printed passives, then fold it accordion-style into a 3D stack bonded at one edge.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6) and capital: no TSVs and known-good-die assembly on roll-to-roll lines, giving cheaper capacity stacks.

title: Prior action: commodity periphery base wafers sold for array build-up
idea: TRIZ #10 Prior action: a merchant foundry pre-manufactures standardized periphery base wafers (sense amps, decoders, pumps and I/O on a fixed grid at 40 nm) in very high volume, and low-capex array companies add only BEOL memory tiers on top, as with gate arrays and structured ASICs.
why: 100x path: array entrants skip ~$15B front-end fabs and periphery design cost, base wafers aim at <$1500 at volume, and BEOL tier lines cost ~$0.5-1B; trade-offs: a fixed periphery limits array flexibility. Attacks capital intensity (Fact 4) and U.S. manufacturability.

title: DSA arrays made defect-tolerant by sense-amp-level remapping
idea: Failure mined: directed self-assembly lithography died in high-volume manufacturing because it could not pattern irregular periphery or hit the ~0.01/cm^2 defect target. Fix: once periphery moves to a bonded logic wafer, the array wafer is purely periodic, which is what block copolymers do well. Each sense-amp group carries a remap table filled at test, so DSA defects (~1/cm^2) are mapped out like bad columns.
why: 10x at the same cost: block copolymers at ~7 nm half-pitch with no EUV give (12/7)^2 = ~3x density, x1.9 from an all-array wafer, x1.5 from regular 4F^2 vertical-channel cells, ~9-10x at lower capital.

title: Three-transistor single-ended sense amp with 60 mV offset accepted
idea: Box: pillar cap x Si access x single-ended skewed-inverter sensing x minimum-size SA x bulk Si x standard. The 8-10 transistor cross-coupled, equalized SA becomes a precharged skewed inverter plus a restore transistor that tolerates ~60 mV offset, so ~1% of bits mis-sense and are fixed downstream.
why: SA area -60%: the SA stripe falls from ~10% to ~4% of die and matched-pair layout rules disappear.

title: Liquid-nitrogen racks with cryo-CMOS periphery and no refresh
idea: Combine datacenter immersion-cooling infrastructure with 77 K operation: access-transistor leakage drops by orders of magnitude so retention reaches hours, and periphery gains ~2x mobility with lower wire resistance; redesign the periphery for 77 K with higher Vt and VDD near 0.6 V.
why: Refresh (fact 3) essentially eliminated and voltage floor (fact 10) relaxed; system energy per bit perhaps ~3x lower even after ~10 W/W cryocooler overhead.

title: Eliminate dummy mats: auto-zeroed self-referenced open-bitline sensing
idea: Remove the reference bitline and the half-populated dummy arrays that 6F2 open-bitline mats need at their edges. Each SA samples its own bitline onto a 2 fF capacitor just before the wordline rises and again after charge sharing, and a switched-capacitor comparator decides on the difference, cancelling SA offset and precharge error in the same step.
why: Edge dummy mats cost ~3-5% of die area; offset cancellation recovers ~30 mV of margin, so Cs can drop ~20% (fact 1) or bitlines can grow longer.

title: Data-polarity rotation balances sense-amp aging over 30 years
idea: Thirty-year industrial parts fail from slow asymmetric drift: the controller inverts stored polarity on alternate refresh epochs (tracked by a per-row flag bit), so both transistors of each SA pair see equal NBTI/PBTI stress and offset stays near zero. SAs can be sized for beginning-of-life margin.
why: SA width ~20% smaller at relaxed DUV rules (fact 7) with no end-of-life guard band.

title: Resonant-tunneling-diode MOBILE latch replaces cross-coupled sense amp
idea: Box: stacked cap x Si access x NDR bistable sensing x heteroepitaxial devices under the bitline x Si x Si/SiGe RTD epitaxy. Two series resonant tunneling diodes clocked by a rising bias (monostable-bistable logic element) fall into one of two states set by a tiny bitline current imbalance, giving a 3-device latch with picosecond decisions.
why: SA area -60% and faster sensing; NDR supplies gain without large matched transistor pairs.

title: Ferroelectric back-gate deep-freezes idle rows' access transistors
idea: Time shift: one switching event per idle episode (minutes to hours) instead of a refresh every 64 ms. A ferroelectric back-gate under each row's access transistors is flipped when the row goes idle, raising Vt ~0.8 V so subthreshold leakage drops ~10^4-10^6 and retention reaches hours; the next access flips it back, and no refresh exists.
why: Kills the leakage tail that forces refresh (fact 3) without a new storage element; ~1 FE cycle per idle episode makes ~10^10 endurance ample.

title: RFID backscatter turns DRAM output into reflection
idea: Borrowed from passive RFID backscatter: the processor sends a continuous carrier down each data line, and the DRAM die only switches a small termination impedance to modulate the reflection, so it needs no output drivers or their supply current.
why: Data movement (fact 5): DRAM-side I/O energy down ~60-80% and I/O driver periphery shrinks; transmit power moves to the cheaper logic-node host.

title: Polyoxometalate redox clusters as molecular gain-cell storage nodes
idea: Molecule-scale jump: a monolayer of polyoxometalate clusters, which hold discrete electrons in deep molecular orbitals, forms the storage layer in the gate stack of a gain FET; writes add or remove 1-2 electrons per cluster at low voltage and the deep levels keep the charge for hours, so no refresh is scheduled.
why: Hours of retention -> zero refresh (fact 3), no capacitor (fact 1), and self-assembly instead of EUV patterning (fact 4).

title: Analog leaky-capacitor activation integrator replaces row-hammer counter tables
idea: Substitute digital SRAM activation-counter tables with a per-row analog integrator: each activate dumps a fixed charge packet onto a small leaky capacitor in the wordline driver, and when a Schmitt detector trips, the neighbors are refreshed. The leak rate itself sets the time window.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): exact per-row tracking at ~2 transistors + 1 cap per row instead of large CAM/SRAM trackers, which fail at 1k-activation thresholds.

title: Leaky-integrator analog counters catch row hammering at activation rate
idea: Design for the extreme user, the attacker: each activation dumps a fixed charge packet onto that row's ~2 fF integrating capacitor in the SWD stripe, which self-leaks with a ~64 ms time constant; a shared comparator checks it on every activation and triggers neighbor refresh past threshold. An analog rate detector replaces SRAM counter tables.
why: Row hammer at ~1k activations (fact 9) tracked for every row with ~0.5% area instead of megabits of counters, and with no counter aliasing.

title: Smartphone pixel binning for leaky rows
idea: Borrowed from phone-camera pixel binning: when a retention monitor flags a weak row pair, the controller switches it to binned mode, where both cells hold the same bit and both wordlines open together to sum charge on the bitline; healthy rows stay at 1 bit per cell.
why: Refresh tail (fact 3): the <=13 fA tail cells stop setting the refresh rate, so the interval can stretch 4-8x for ~1-2% capacity.

title: Cochlear tonotopic row selection with frequency-addressed wordline groups
idea: Like the basilar membrane, where each position resonates at its own frequency, each local wordline-driver group gets a tiny on-die resonator (BAW/MEMS or LC) tuned to a unique frequency. The bank broadcasts one tone burst on a single shared line, and only the matching group rectifies it into a wordline enable, replacing predecode buses and one decoder level.
why: Fact 7: collapsing 64-way selection onto one wire could cut that decode level's area 30-50% and remove predecode bus switching energy.

title: Po: weakest cousins schedule refresh — canary-cell mats
idea: Po: memory that is told when to refresh by its weakest relatives. Each mat holds one row of canary cells with deliberately shrunk capacitors (~60% Cs), sensed by the normal SAs at each refresh; the mat's refresh interval doubles while all canaries hold and halves on the first canary failure, tracking process and temperature automatically.
why: Refresh (#3): most mats can run 2-4x longer intervals, cutting refresh energy and the 10-20% bandwidth loss at <0.2% area, with per-mat rather than per-die worst-case margins.

title: Eliminate transistor sense latches: carbon-released NEMS bistable beams
idea: Each bitline pair drives the two electrodes of a ~2 um buckled TiN nano-beam above it. The charge-share imbalance plus a common pull-in bias snaps the beam to one side, where its contact pulls that bitline to the rail. The cavity is cut by O2-ashing an amorphous-carbon sacrificial layer, which replaces HF-vapor or XeF2 release.
why: Gives a sense latch with zero leakage and no Vt mismatch, stacked in BEOL over the bitlines (SA area -30%) at ~fJ per sense. Mechanical speed (10-50 ns) restricts it to dense, slow tiers.

title: Braided trio bitlines with permutation-coded, reference-free sensing
idea: Like a three-strand braid, route three bitlines that rotate positions every few cells so all see identical coupling. Store data as the rank order of three distinct charge levels across three cells (6 permutations = 2.58 bits per 3 cells) and read it with three pairwise comparators and no mid-rail reference.
why: Common-mode leakage shifts all three cells together, so rank order survives ~2-4x longer: refresh power drops and reference-generation circuits leave the periphery, at a ~14% raw density cost.

title: Downhole-oil-tool SiC electronics make refresh-free hot memory
idea: Borrowed from SiC electronics in oil-well logging tools and EV inverters: cells and CMOS periphery are built on 4H-SiC wafers (bandgap 3.26 eV), whose intrinsic carrier density is ~1e16x lower than silicon's, so junction leakage stays negligible at 150-200 C beside accelerators.
why: Refresh (fact 3): retention of minutes to hours removes refresh engines and cooling needs, using U.S. SiC wafer capacity built for EVs.

title: Breathing mat back-plate lowers wordline swing to 1.3 V
idea: The 3 V wordline exists only because Vt must be high for retention. Make Vt dynamic: a mat-shared back-gate plate sits at -1 V in standby (deep off, leakage tail suppressed) and steps to 0 V only for the accessed mat, so the wordline needs ~1.3 V and its drivers become thin-oxide core devices.
why: Voltage floor and periphery (facts 7, 10): wordline CV^2 energy ~5x lower ((3/1.3)^2), driver area ~3x smaller, charge pump eliminated or shrunk.

title: Po: rust-and-zinc logic above the array — Cu2O/ZnO CMOS
idea: Po: periphery made of rust and zinc. Build complementary BEOL thin-film logic from p-type Cu2O and n-type Al-doped ZnO (no In or Ga) to host refresh counters, mode registers, test and redundancy logic stacked above the cell array.
why: Periphery (#7) and scarce resources: shifts ~5-8% of slow control logic into vertical space using only Cu, Zn, Al, O, avoiding IGZO's indium and gallium.

title: Geiger-mode avalanche junction as a digital charge-threshold detector
idea: Substitute the regenerative latch with an implanted silicon p-n junction biased just below avalanche (as in SPAD pixels) with a quench resistor: the bitline signal pushes it over breakdown or not, giving a full-swing digital output in ~100 ps. Implant, anneal and contact are basic nanofab steps.
why: Charge wall and SA area: avalanche gain of 10^5 or more resolves femtocoulomb signals in one compact junction plus resistor.
